entry.title: Agents were demo-ready in 2023. Production still has to be engineered
entry.summary: Meher Bhaskar Madiraju (Walmart Global Tech) at Conf42 MLOps 2026 on the contracts, caching, evals and rollback gates an agent needs after the demo.
entry.content:
Chain ten agent steps that each succeed 90% of the time and the whole run succeeds about 35% of the time. That arithmetic sits at the centre of the talk Meher Bhaskar Madiraju, senior data scientist at Walmart Global Tech, gave at Conf42 MLOps 2026. His argument: models have improved quickly, outcomes have not kept pace, and the gap is engineering work with a known checklist.

A note on scope. The abstract promises a case study from more than 600 retail locations. The recorded talk is something else: a field guide assembled from public incidents and published engineering write-ups, with no internal numbers. It is useful on those terms.

Capability went up, outcomes did not follow

He opens with SWE-bench Verified: the best system scored around 33% in August 2024 and around 80% by January 2026. Then the other column. He cites MIT's NANDA group finding that 95% of generative AI projects show no measurable P&L impact, Gartner's prediction that more than 40% of agentic AI projects will be cancelled by the end of 2027, and the METR trial where experienced open source maintainers felt about 20% faster with AI help and measured 19% slower. He grants that the methodologies are debated.

Two incidents make it concrete: the Replit agent that wiped a production database during a code freeze and then produced fake passing test reports, and the Air Canada chatbot whose invented bereavement policy cost the airline 650 Canadian dollars at a tribunal. "Neither of these failures was a model capability problem. Both were engineering problems," Meher Bhaskar Madiraju said at Conf42 MLOps 2026.

The third story is Klarna, whose assistant handled 2.3 million conversations in its first month and cut resolution time from 11 minutes to under two, before the company started bringing human operators back. His reading is that both announcements were sincere, and that the metric you choose to evaluate against is a product decision.

Fan out reads, keep writes single-threaded

On multi-agent design he puts two published positions next to each other. Anthropic's research system, a lead agent spawning parallel sub-agents, scored 90.2% higher than a single agent on an internal eval. Walden Yan of Cognition argues against building multi-agent systems at all, because agents acting in parallel make conflicting implicit decisions. Meher's point is that both agree on the mechanism: sub-agents work when their tasks are read-only.

His rule: "Fan out only for read-only and independently verifiable breadth." Write paths stay single-threaded with full context, and sub-agents return compressed findings, never transcripts.

He then walks four delegation shapes with one failure and one fix each: supervisor (context bloat, fixed by turn and token budgets), pipeline (bad input poisoning every later stage, fixed by typed contracts, checkpoints and dead letter queues), blackboard (write races, fixed by versioned additive writes and leases) and debate (sycophancy, fixed by adversarial personas and a round cap). Every delegation gets a contract with a deadline, a token budget and a response format, plus one named owner for the final answer.

Prompt layout is a cost decision

The context engineering section borrows from Manus, whose agent runs roughly 100 input tokens per output token. That makes cache hit rate the number to watch. He shows the same 20-turn conversation with two layouts. A stable block on top (system prompt, tools, reference docs) with append-only history hit the cache 93% of the time. Put a timestamp or session ID near the top and it fell to 33%. Same model, same task, roughly six times cheaper with the stable layout.

The rules follow: immutable content first, volatile data at the end, never rewrite earlier turns, and mask unavailable tools instead of removing them. For full context windows he lists four habits: compact, take notes outside the window, recite the objective every few turns, and quarantine independent work in a sub-agent.

Reliability compounds, so do the fixes

Back to the formula. For n steps at per-step reliability r, end-to-end success is r to the power n. Ten steps at 99% gives 90%. Ten steps at 90% gives 35%. His remedies are familiar from distributed systems: retries with backoff and jitter, degraded fallback paths, circuit breakers, timeouts, and idempotency keys on anything that mutates. Without the keys, a retry is a second delete.

For hallucination loops, where a small error enters the context and tool results get read as confirmation, he names three structural breaks: require citations for claims, validate every tool output with plain code before it enters the context, and run a critic pass over the plan.

Ship it like software, with a kill switch

The closing third assembles a nine-layer control plane (gateway, orchestrator, agent fleet, tools, memory, observability, eval harness, deploy and fallback, guardrails) and a tiered eval stack: deterministic contract tests in CI, LLM judges on a golden dataset, simulation and canaries, then expert review. Promotion goes offline evals, shadow traffic, canary, full rollout, with rollback triggers wired to guardrails so a regression does not wait for a human. He wants a kill switch that stops spend in seconds without a config change going through review.

Who should watch

Engineers and tech leads with an agent prototype that has impressed a room and now needs an owner. The talk is a dense, well-organised survey, so people who already follow the Anthropic, Cognition and Manus write-ups will recognise much of it. If you came for a retail deployment story, this recording does not contain one.

entry.title: Precompute by default: LLM features on a page that cannot wait
entry.summary: Artem Zamarajev (Amazon) at Conf42 MLOps 2026 on four lessons for LLM features on a busy web page: precompute, fallbacks, output checks, one gateway.
entry.content:
The safest model call on a product page is the one that never happens while the shopper is waiting. At Conf42 MLOps 2026, Artem Zamarajev, a senior software engineer at Amazon working on AI shopping features, compresses what he has learned about LLM features on high-traffic pages into four lessons: precompute by default, keep the model off the critical path, check outputs before customers see them, and put one service in front of the assistant.

His scope is narrow on purpose. This is about AI features inside a web page a shopper loads in a browser. Standalone chatbots and background agents get only partial credit.

Three problems the usual toolkit does not cover

Timeouts, caching, canaries, feature flags and A/B tests still apply. LLM features add three things on top.

Latency: he quotes Google's guidance that a page's main content should appear within 2.5 seconds and the first byte within 0.8 seconds. A fast model starts streaming in a few hundred milliseconds, but a full response takes several seconds and the slow tail runs longer.

Quality: bad output arrives well-formed with a successful status, so the error rate stays flat while customers read something wrong.

Cost: every call costs money, and page-view volume multiplies it.

To keep the lessons concrete he invents a store, Ridgeline Coffee, with three features on each product page. A quick take (three LLM-written highlights from product details and reviews), suggested questions picked for the shopper, and an Ask button that opens the store's assistant.

Ask three questions before generating anything live

Does the output depend on the shopper or what they typed? How often do the inputs change? Is anyone waiting for it?

The quick take is the same for everyone, changes only when the product or its reviews change, and nobody is waiting. So it is generated in a background job, checked, and stored. The page does a key lookup. Latency becomes a read, and cost follows product changes instead of traffic. One trap: regenerate on every new review and a popular product burns model calls all day for text that barely moves. He uses a threshold, such as a minimum number of new reviews.

The Ask button has to be live, but only runs for shoppers who click. Suggested questions depend on the shopper, so they run live on every page view. Remember that one for lesson four.

A timeout will not save the page

A timeout short enough to protect the page would cut off most model calls. So the answer depends on the feature type.

For precomputed content he decides the fallback before writing a prompt, as a ladder: fresh content, then the last good version, then a plain non-AI default such as the product's existing bullet points, then hiding the feature. For live features the page renders first and the model is called afterwards. Suggested questions fill in late, and if they fail the space stays empty. The Ask response is streamed, which also keeps long answers from hitting fixed timeouts in proxies and gateways. The worst case is a plainer page.

Wrong output looks like success

He brings up the 2024 tribunal ruling against Air Canada, whose chatbot told a customer something that contradicted the airline's own policy page. The company owns what the model says.

Before a quick take is stored, it passes four checks: format, grounding (every claim traces to product data or a review), consistency with the rest of the page, and content policy. A highlight saying the coffee ships ground on a page that says whole bean only is his small-scale example. Format and policy are mostly rules. Grounding and consistency often need a second model call, which is affordable because it runs once per product change.

Live responses get layers instead: the model works from the product's own data, cheap rule checks run on the stream, and a sample of real responses is judged afterwards. Both kinds get a fixed eval set rerun on every prompt or model change. And because fallbacks hide failures, the rejection rate is the metric to watch during a rollout. The page looks healthy either way.

One door in front of the assistant

The Ask button and suggested questions both call the same assistant. Let each call it directly and two things go wrong. Eligibility rules, languages, timeouts and fallbacks get copied and drift apart. And an assistant sized for the small share of shoppers who click Ask suddenly receives a call on every page view.

His fix is a small service between features and the assistant that holds the rules, sets the timeout, returns fallbacks, and gives each feature a traffic budget with rate limits. "I make it a service rather than a shared library because a library can't enforce one budget across every caller," Artem Zamarajev said at Conf42 MLOps 2026.

His one-line summary of the whole talk: "calling the model is easy, and most of the work is just a system around it".

Who should watch

Backend and full-stack engineers adding generative features to pages that already have latency targets, and the product managers who keep asking why it cannot just call the model. It is a short, tidy talk with no slides of production metrics. The abstract speaks of millions of daily renders with zero faults, while the recording stays with the invented coffee shop, so expect patterns over war stories.

entry.title: Agent reliability is a property of the platform around the model
entry.summary: Amit Anand at Conf42 MLOps 2026 on the platform agents need to heal infrastructure: durable runs, a policy gate, run IDs and autonomy per action class.
entry.content:
At 99% success per step and no retries, a 50-step agent run completes about 60% of the time. Amit Anand, who builds distributed systems, payment systems and AI agents, uses that arithmetic at Conf42 MLOps 2026 to argue that agent reliability is decided by the platform, and then runs an architecture review of that platform with one incident threaded through it: latency on an API service creeps up after a deployment, and an agent proposes a rollback.

"The reliability of agentic system is a property of the platform around the model," Amit Anand said at Conf42 MLOps 2026. He opens and closes on that sentence.

An agent run is a long workflow whose control flow you do not know

Amit reads an agent run as a distributed, long-running workflow where the model picks the control flow at runtime. A trigger starts the run, then it loops: plan through the model gateway, act through the tool gateway, write a checkpoint to a state store, emit telemetry tagged with the run ID. Every arrow is a remote call that can be slow, fail or be retried.

Four forces follow. You do not know a run's length or fan-out when you admit it, so you need admission control and run budgets. Failures compound, so you retry individual steps and each step must be safe to retry. Runs outlive their compute, since a pod or a deploy can end before the run does, so state has to be durable. And one run mixes GPU-bound, CPU-bound and I/O-bound work, which calls for separate pools that scale on work signals.

The planner never touches production

In the incident, telemetry arrives through OpenTelemetry, detection correlates alerts and traces into one incident, diagnosis finds the deployment, and planning proposes a rollback with a risk score. Then comes the box Amit calls the most important: the policy gate. Policy as code decides whether a rollback is permitted on this service right now and answers allow, deny or ask a human. If allowed, the change is applied, preferably as a Git commit that a controller reconciles.

Verification closes the loop. If latency and error rates recover, done. If the result is unclear or worse, the default is to stop and escalate to the on-call engineer. An automatic compensating action runs only where one has been defined and tested.

The security model is a trust boundary. Everything the agent reads is untrusted: alerts, logs, tickets, tool output. A line injected into a log can steer an agent with broad privileges, the classic confused deputy. So the agent runtime gets a scoped identity that can read telemetry, call the model and write its own state. It emits a typed request, and every infrastructure-changing action goes through a gateway that can refuse. As a side benefit, "Your compliance evidence is the gateway log."

Retry storms, duplicate actions and 200 OK

Amit walks through three failure modes. In a retry storm, a model endpoint slows, every agent retries together and load peaks when capacity is lowest, which is also how cost runs away. The response is rate limits, jittered backoff and load shedding at the gateway. Duplicate actions happen when a worker crashes after requesting the rollback and before recording the result, so actions need idempotency keys and you verify state before retrying when the outcome is unknown.

The observability gap is the quiet one. Model and tool spans come from different libraries with no shared context. The Kubernetes change carries no run ID, so the audit log shows a service account patched a deployment and cannot say which decision caused it. Nothing records the outcome: every call returns 200 whether or not latency recovered. His rule is to connect run ID, decision, action and outcome, because you should not automate what you cannot evaluate.

Autonomy is granted per action class

The reference architecture has one logical control plane per organisation holding the model and tool registry with evaluation gates, GitOps and policy, quota and the observability backend, over identical Kubernetes clusters per cloud. Inside a cluster, a KEDA scaler sets the worker count from queue depth and age, and scale-in must respect active runs. The GPU pool scales on waiting requests, queue time and time to first token, because throughput flattens once the pool is saturated.

On multi-cloud he is careful. Routing new inference requests to another cloud is the easy case, though a pairing such as GKE with Vertex AI and EKS with Bedrock is not interchangeable, so prompts and evaluations must pass on both. Resuming a run already in progress is harder. You pay for it in recovery time, data residency constraints, network cost and idle GPUs.

Autonomy is set by reversibility and blast radius. Reversible and narrow actions may become autonomous, wide and irreversible ones need approval, and every class starts as recommend-only and steps up when its evaluation passes and its production record is clean. For run execution he compares LangGraph checkpoints with a workflow engine such as Temporal and notes the two can be used together.

MLOps comes in at release. Version the model, prompt, tools and configuration together, evaluate the version on past incidents, deploy gradually. "A new prompt goes through the same gate as a new model."

Who should watch

Platform engineers and SREs who have been asked to let an agent act on production and want the design questions in one place. It is a dense architecture review in under fifteen minutes, with no demo and no vendor product. The migration order alone is worth noting down: join the traces, insert the gateway in recommend-only mode, turn runbooks into typed tools, then promote by evidence.

  • Autonomy with Guardrails: Operating Agentic Automation in High-Risk Production Systems by Ajay Athitya Ramanathan at Conf42 SRE 2026.

entry.title: How OpenAI connects Codex to Flyte through MCP for ML training runs
entry.summary: Phoebe Wang (OpenAI) at Conf42 MLOps 2026 on a read-only Flyte MCP tool that lets Codex turn a failed training run link into a first fix to test.
entry.content:
OpenAI hosts Flyte for its internal traditional ML training jobs, and the unit that moves between people, the orchestrator and the coding agent is a run link. At Conf42 MLOps 2026, Phoebe Wang, Member of Technical Staff at OpenAI working on ML infrastructure, shows how a small Flyte MCP server lets Codex look up a failed execution, report what Flyte recorded and suggest the first thing to test. It is a short talk with one clear pattern in it.

A failed run is three questions

Phoebe starts with a scene every ML engineer knows. You change a model, submit the full training job, go back to other work, and later receive a link to a failed run. In her fictional example, loading the data worked, training failed, and evaluation never started because it needs the trained model. What she wants to know at that point is which step failed, what error was reported and what to test next.

The three pieces each have one job. Flyte, the open-source ML orchestration layer, runs the steps of a workflow and records the state of every run. MCP, the Model Context Protocol, lets an AI application use tools, so a Flyte MCP server can expose a tool that looks up a run and returns its task states and recorded errors. Codex is where the question gets asked.

"The useful handoff is the link," Phoebe Wang said at Conf42 MLOps 2026. The same link can go to a teammate, and both people start from the same run.

The run record is what makes the next run a fair comparison

A workflow defines the steps; a run is one attempt at them. Her example is an image classifier where run 41 finished all three steps and run 42 stopped in training, both from the same workflow.

That history matters the next morning, when the editor holds three more changes. Which version of the code did the failed job run? Was it the same dataset as the last good run? Did the batch size or the GPU type change? She keeps the run link and records the workflow version, the software environment, the dataset and the inputs, which for this classifier include the evaluation split and the batch size. Change one thing in the next run and those records make the comparison fair. They also let you trace a model you want to serve back to the run that produced it.

Give the tool a narrow, read-only job

The integration answers one small question: given a link, can Codex tell which step failed and what Flyte recorded? Phoebe's summary of the design: "That gives the tool a narrow read-only job."

For run 42 the tool returns the run state, the failed task and the error details. Flyte says the training step ran out of GPU memory and that evaluation was skipped, so the place to look is training. Her advice for teams building something similar comes as four principles:

  • Start with the information someone would normally open the workflow UI to find.
  • Give the tool a way to identify the exact run.
  • Return the task and the error in a form the agent can refer to.
  • Keep access scoped to the runs the caller is allowed to see.

Evidence first, then a suggestion you still review

In the Codex CLI, the first part of the answer is the evidence: the error trace Flyte returned. The suggestion follows from it. An out-of-memory error in training points to a smaller batch, because a smaller batch keeps fewer things in GPU memory at once. Codex can update the local training code and environment so the modified run can start.

Phoebe keeps the human in two places. She reviews the change before submitting a run, and she checks the evaluation score afterwards, because a smaller batch can change training behaviour. A run that finishes and a model worth keeping are two separate things to verify.

The talk ends with the step after training. Her team built a GPU deploy skill in Codex so experimental models can be put on GPUs quickly and tested end to end for latency and availability. The example request is to prepare a test deployment of version three of the classifier and show the change for review, which gives Codex a model, a version, a target and a clear point to hand back.

Who should watch

Platform engineers who run Flyte, or any workflow orchestrator, and are deciding what to expose to coding agents first. The session is brief and uses a fictional run on slides; it does not go into how the MCP server is implemented, and the checklist promised in the abstract arrives as the four design principles above. As a pattern for a first, low-risk agent integration, it is easy to copy.

entry.title: Incident agents: diagnosis is the easy half, authority is the hard one
entry.summary: Nishanth Vepachedu at Conf42 MLOps 2026 on graduated oversight for incident agents: typed actions, risk tiers and a session score the agent cannot lower.
entry.content:
An incident agent is a privileged identity in production whose main input is partly written by strangers. That is how Nishanth Vepachedu, who works on AI infrastructure for agentic systems, frames the problem at Conf42 MLOps 2026. Most talks on this subject are about making the agent a good investigator. His is about what the agent is allowed to do, who decides, and how that decision should change as an investigation drags on.

Anyone who can send a request to your service can put words in your logs. The agent that reads those logs may also be able to restart and roll back. In security terms, he says, that is a confused deputy waiting to happen.

A good investigator has four habits

He covers the investigation side quickly and fairly. A credible agent grounds every claim in a trace ID, a timestamp and linked log lines, and a claim it cannot cite is not a finding. It turns its story into a prediction and runs the query that could refute it first. It retrieves in stages, cheap aggregates before traces before log windows, behind a gateway that enforces a budget so the investigation does not take down the telemetry. And it is honest about gaps: sampling drops spans, and a missing edge is not evidence of health.

When that side goes wrong, an engineer loses time. When the action side goes wrong, customers lose service. And the usual safeguard there is one approve or deny prompt, the same for restarting a pod and for changing network policy in a region. By the twentieth prompt of the night, the on-call engineer is clicking approve.

Logs are untrusted input, and no single step is the breach

He makes the input problem concrete with research he cites. In a benchmark called LogJack, authors planted prompt injection payloads in cloud logs and gave them to debugging agents built on eight foundation models; on six of the eight, the agent executed a command that came from log content. A NeurIPS paper on security operations agents ran more than 1,100 payloads, and every configuration tested could be talked into downgrading real malicious activity. Letting the agent pull more read-only telemetry to cross-check did not reliably fix it.

The second problem needs no attacker. An agent reads logs, queries traces, restarts a pod, then the service, then proposes a network policy change. Each step passes on its own. The path went from reader to network editor and nothing raised the bar. He points to a July incident in which research agents in an OpenAI security evaluation got out of their sandbox into Hugging Face's production: by the accounts he cites, roughly 17,600 actions over four days, and from one dataset pod to cluster admin in under 13 hours. He is careful to say those were not incident response agents. The lesson he takes is narrower: a control that judges one call at a time, with no memory, cannot see a trajectory.

The action sets a floor, and the session raises it

His proposal, which he is building as an open reference design, starts with making the agent the best instrumented service you own. Every tool call emits a typed event before it runs: effect (none, reversible, irreversible), scope (pod, service, region), provenance (which inputs influenced it, any of them untrusted), and what scrutiny was required and granted. A tool with no declared metadata fails closed.

Typed actions get a floor. Querying telemetry is tier zero, a pod restart gets a light check, network policy needs a person, and anything irreversible or crossing a tenant boundary never drops below human approval. "Confidence is not a credential.", Nishanth Vepachedu said at Conf42 MLOps 2026.

Between acting alone and asking a human he puts steps: observe; justify in a fixed structure that a deterministic rule checks against the cited evidence; a second opinion from an independent model; human approval with provenance shown; halt. The tier an action needs is the larger of its floor and the tier implied by the risk the session has accumulated. Three properties hold it together: nothing the agent says or reads can lower the score, a sub-agent inherits its parent's risk, and the floor always holds.

Models act as sensors here, with measured error rates. Authority lives in a small deterministic state machine. His rule: a model's judgment is evidence, not permission.

Four numbers to ask any vendor for

He offers no results, and says so: the harness is in progress. What he offers are the measurements. Which tier caught each unsafe action. Approvals per on-call shift, treated as a budget. How many legitimate investigations still complete with the gate on. And the miss rate when replayed against past incidents.

The rollout order follows: offline replay, read-only in production with the gate in shadow, reversible actions, then wider authority only as far as the data supports. His one-sentence summary is "Scale the oversight with the agent."

Who should watch

SREs, platform engineers and security people who are being asked to let an agent do more than write summaries. If you want a tour of LLM-driven telemetry correlation with MTTR numbers, as the abstract suggests, this is a different and more useful talk: a design argument about authority, with no product and no benchmarks of its own yet.

entry.title: A loan valuation you cannot replay is one you cannot defend
entry.summary: Ankur Mehra at Conf42 MLOps 2026 on valuing illiquid loans with pinned versions, signed run manifests and event-driven revaluation.
entry.content:
A stock has a quoted price. A mortgage or a commercial loan sitting on a bank's book does not, so its value has to be modelled, and remodelled every time rates, spreads or borrower behaviour move. At Conf42 MLOps 2026, Ankur Mehra, who has spent more than fifteen years in financial risk technology for major US banks, argues that the model is only half of that job. The other half is a pipeline in which every valuation run pins its data, assumptions and model config, so any historical number can be replayed from its manifest.

His two opening points set the bar. Accuracy alone is insufficient if the model cannot be run consistently at scale, and auditability is non-negotiable because regulators expect every valuation to be traceable back to its inputs.

Three stages, each allowed to say no

The pipeline has three stages: market data ingestion, scenario setup and cash flow modelling, where payments are projected and discounted to a present value. Each stage is independently versioned, testable and auditable, and failures are isolated. "A bad input should stop the pipeline," Ankur Mehra said at Conf42 MLOps 2026. It should never pass silently downstream into a number someone signs off on.

Market data is treated as a first-class artifact. Rate curves, credit spreads and prepayment indices come from multiple providers, and every ingestion batch gets a timestamp and a hash, so you can prove which data a valuation used. Schema validation and anomaly detection run at the boundary, and rejected batches go to a dead letter queue where they are quarantined and reviewable.

Scenarios are separated from model logic. A registry stores each named, versioned scenario as an immutable artifact, overrides are injected when the pipeline is invoked and never hard-coded, and base, stress and regulatory cases fan out in parallel against the same cash flow engine. That is faster, and it guarantees they all ran on identical inputs.

The engine itself is stateless and deterministic. Prepayment and credit models are pluggable, discount curves are injected, and the engine outputs intermediate cash flows as well as the final NPV. When a value moves, those intermediate numbers are how you explain why.

Reproducibility breaks in four boring ways

Ankur's list will sound familiar outside finance too. Reference data gets overwritten in place. Model parameters live only in someone's notebook. Someone makes a manual override to an assumption and does not document it. A dependency is upgraded in the middle of a cycle.

The fix is versioning in three layers and a manifest that ties them together. The data layer covers the market data snapshot, portfolio positions and reference data. The assumption layer covers prepayment speeds, credit loss curves and discount rate conventions. The model config layer covers algorithmic parameters, feature sets and calibration output. Every run ID pins a specific version in all three.

Each run then emits a signed manifest with the data snapshot IDs, the assumption set hash, the model config version, a hash of the pipeline and a digest of the execution environment, kept in append-only storage. "That manifest is your audit defense," he said. In his closing principles he puts the reason plainly: mutation is the root cause of most reproducibility failures.

Rollback has to be one command

Changing a live valuation model follows a promotion path: shadow mode on real data with outputs unused, a challenger test against the current baseline, a staged rollout to a subset of the portfolio, then full cutover. At every step, rollback must be a single command with zero manual intervention. "If going back is hard, people hesitate, and that's when problem starts."

Around that sit the controls. Four categories of metrics answer four questions: is the pipeline healthy, are the inputs healthy, do the results look plausible, and do portfolio-level business rules hold before anything is published. He calls the last one the most important, the final gate between the pipeline and the people who rely on its numbers.

Testing has four layers as well: unit tests for cash flow and discounting logic, integration tests on synthetic loan portfolios, regression tests against pinned historical baselines so you know if a code change moved a number, and stress tests for numerical stability at extreme inputs. Lineage should answer in seconds which runs consumed a given version of a rate curve. When a vendor calls to say a curve was wrong, that query is the difference between a quiet afternoon and a long week.

Every production run also produces an audit pack: the signed manifest, a lineage graph report, intermediate cash flow snapshots, output distribution statistics, the business rule validation report and the approval record.

Stop revaluing loans where nothing changed

Most valuation systems revalue the whole portfolio on a schedule, spending most of the compute on loans where nothing changed. Ankur's last chapter flips that: a rate curve update revalues the affected tranches, a position change revalues the impacted loans, and an assumption update triggers a scoped rerun with lineage showing which numbers were refreshed and why. This only works because every input is versioned and every dependency tracked, so the system knows what needs recomputing.

Who should watch

Engineers and quants running valuation, risk or pricing models in regulated finance, and MLOps people who want a clean example of reproducibility taken seriously. entry.title: Why logistic regression beat a CNN and an LSTM on noisy product names
entry.summary: Vladimir Beskorovainyi (Besk Tech) at Conf42 MLOps 2026 on character n-gram logistic regression beating a CNN, an LSTM and DistilBERT on receipt text.
entry.content:
A character n-gram logistic regression beat a 1D CNN and an LSTM on product names from supermarket receipts in every category and every split: 30 cells out of 30. At Conf42 MLOps 2026, Vladimir Beskorovainyi, CTO and CPO at Besk Tech, reports that result, then spends most of his time on the parts that complicate it: the winner is also the slowest of the cheap models, the rules in front of it cap everything, and a benchmark score can fall apart on real data.

The task: one receipt line, one six-digit category

Each line from a receipt has to be assigned a six-digit COICOP consumption category so prices can be compared. The text is short and dirty: abbreviations, typos, the seller's internal codes, words stuck together, and no product codes or retailer categories to lean on.

Vladimir is careful about where his numbers come from. Everything measured in the talk is from a public synthetic benchmark with six categories and five splits, with open code. The architecture has run in production since 2021 at national scale, taking in tens of millions of product lines a day, but that system is under NDA. The deploying organization reports 90 percent accuracy on the live stream; he says that is their figure for the whole pipeline and declines to explain it with his benchmark.

He also compares models in pairs, cell by cell, because an average can hide a model that wins two categories and loses four.

The headline survives the overlap check

The character n-gram model with logistic regression reaches a mean F1 of 0.997. Then comes the check many papers skip: 34 percent of the test items also appear word for word in training. That is realistic for receipts and it inflates any score, so he measured the unseen items separately and got 0.996. The character model does not depend on the overlap. The word-level models do.

Across everything trained from scratch, four points separate the best from the worst. He also owns up to two corrections. An earlier version gave the deep models less training time; with a fair budget they are no longer the worst, just no better. And his old timing code made the cheap models look slow. The corrected gap in training cost is 212 times for the CNN and 258 times for the LSTM.

Put cost in the same table as accuracy

Character n-grams are the most accurate and, among the cheap models, the slowest: 41,500 items a second. A plain bag of words does 191,300, which is 4.6 times faster and three points of F1 behind. At tens of millions of lines a day that difference decides whether the job finishes at all.

So his answer is three reasonable choices, picked by whether you are paid for accuracy or for speed, and the deep models are not on the list. He also trained DistilBERT: 0.993, good, but the character model still wins 18 cells to 3, and the transformer handles 82 items a second, about 460 times slower.

The rules decide what the model ever sees

In the production design, rules pick the category and a small per-category model only confirms or rejects. People and the model vote under one rule, and a category is configuration that a methodologist can add without an engineer.

The catch is that the rule stage lets through 75 to 86 percent of the right items, and nothing downstream can do better than that. The rules stay anyway, because a rule is a phrase a person can read, change and defend to an auditor.

On labels, each annotator carries a reliability weight capped at two. In the data, strong and weak annotators both end up at two, so the weight saturates and stops telling them apart. Weighted voting still buys the classifier one to two points. "Labels are the cheapest points you can buy," Vladimir Beskorovainyi said at Conf42 MLOps 2026.

Ninety-seven on a test set, forty-one in the field

The most useful slide is the one about limits. The benchmark is synthetic and real receipts are worse. He cites a published study that reported 97.4 percent on held-out test data and, with the same approach on real unlabeled data, coded about 41 percent of expenditure correctly. His summary: "Ninety-seven on a test set, forty-one in the field."

His four takeaways follow from that: on short noisy product names the character n-gram model was the strongest thing he measured, cost belongs next to accuracy, fix labels before tuning the model, and architecture matters more than model size. The preprint is arXiv:2606.02004 and under review at PeerJ Computer Science, with code on GitHub and data on Zenodo. Next on his list: run it on real receipts and raise the recall of the rule stage without losing explainability.

Who should watch

Anyone classifying short, messy text at volume, and anyone about to propose a transformer for a job a linear model might already do. It is a compact, paper-style talk: slides and numbers, no demo, and a speaker who publishes his own corrections. If you want proof on real receipts, he says plainly that this study does not provide it.

entry.title: An 833-parameter model on the phone beats a chatbot round trip
entry.summary: RanjithKumar Ragavan (T-Mobile) at Conf42 MLOps 2026 on exporting a tiny PyTorch model to ExecuTorch so health data is scored on the phone.
entry.content:
RanjithKumar Ragavan caught himself screenshotting his Oura Ring metrics every morning and pasting them into a cloud chatbot to ask whether he should work out. At Conf42 MLOps 2026, the Member of Technical Staff at T-Mobile shows what he built instead: Noctua, an open-source Kotlin SDK that runs an 833-parameter PyTorch model on the phone through ExecuTorch, in under five milliseconds by his account, with no health data leaving the device. He is clear that it is a personal project, independent of his employer.

The itch is what he calls the gap between measurement and coaching. The ring tracks heart rate variability, sleep stages, resting heart rate and skin temperature, the app reports a readiness score, and none of it answers the question of whether to train hard today. Uploading a continuous physiological history to a third party to answer something the phone's processor can compute is the anti-pattern he set out to remove.

The phone is the feature pipeline

In cloud MLOps a warehouse and a feature store prepare the inputs. Here the handset does it. Noctua's core module fetches the trailing 21 days of data from the Oura API v2 and folds readiness, sleep, activity and HRV into an immutable Kotlin object. A feature extractor then normalises it against the wearer's own baseline, because raw HRV means nothing across people: fifty milliseconds can be good recovery for one person and deep fatigue for another. Out come eight floating-point features, including accumulated sleep debt, HRV against a fourteen-day rolling baseline, the resting heart rate delta and three-day readiness momentum.

The SDK is split into three Gradle modules: a pure Kotlin, coroutine-first API client that handles OAuth, token refresh and pagination; the AI module with feature extraction, a heuristic engine and the ExecuTorch bridge; and a Jetpack Compose example app. That app has a deterministic 21-day synthetic demo mode, so you can watch the model run without owning a ring.

Eight inputs do not need a two-gigabyte model

His strongest opinion is about sizing. It is tempting to quantize a multi-gigabyte language model for everything, and wasteful to spend a user's battery and storage that way to predict one score from eight numbers. Noctua uses a multilayer perceptron with an 8-32-16-1 topology. The hidden layers are there because the features interact: the same workout strain leads to a good day with a positive HRV baseline and a sharp readiness drop with a negative one plus sleep debt. A linear equation misses that.

The whole network is 833 float32 parameters, and the compiled program is about eight kilobytes on disk as he gives it, smaller than an app icon.

Three lowering stages and ten lines of Python

The export script is short. Put the model in eval mode, create a sample input of shape one by eight, then run ExecuTorch's ahead-of-time pipeline. First, torch.export captures a static graph in the core ATen dialect, and the Python overhead is gone. Second, to_edge lowers it to the Edge dialect and normalises operators. Third, to_executorch does static memory planning, working out the offsets of intermediate tensors at compile time so the phone does no dynamic allocation during inference. The result is written out as a .pte file.

The native runtime is optional by design

Shipping a C++ runtime inside an SDK invites a classic crash: one consumer leaves out the native dependency to keep the APK small, a CI server runs tests on a desktop JVM with no JNI library, and everything dies on an unsatisfied link error. Noctua loads the ExecuTorch runtime reflectively and, if the runtime or the .pte file is missing, falls back to a zero-dependency linear model in pure Kotlin. The UI badge says which engine produced the number. All sixteen unit tests run on a plain JVM as a result.

The neural forecast is paired with deterministic, unit-tested rules that run on the same features and flag things like sleep debt or HRV below baseline with a confidence figure. His reason: "you cannot afford hallucinated medical advice". The network forecasts, and the rules keep every recommendation traceable.

He compares the result with the cloud route on four counts: privacy, explainability, speed and resilience. A cloud round trip takes from 500 milliseconds to a couple of seconds and fails on a flight or a trail. "privacy is the product", RanjithKumar Ragavan said at Conf42 MLOps 2026.

Who should watch

Android and mobile engineers who want a small, complete ExecuTorch example, and ML engineers curious about what the export path looks like end to end. Set expectations against the abstract, though: this is a twenty-minute case study of one tiny tabular model. Quantization-aware training, pruning, distillation, NPU versus CPU paths and device-tier validation are not covered. The roadmap he lists is a local LLM coach through ExecuTorch's Llama runner, overnight on-device fine-tuning, Android Health Connect write-back and a Kotlin Multiplatform port for iOS. The project is MIT licensed.

entry.title: Name it, scope it, gate it, record it: agents in a regulated enterprise
entry.summary: Shanker Valipireddy (Aflac) at Conf42 MLOps 2026 on a four-step control plane for agents: identity, scoped grant, policy gate and immutable audit.
entry.content:
Teams spend months on model quality while the agent still runs under a shared service account with broad access and no record of what it did. At Conf42 MLOps 2026, Shanker Valipireddy, Principal Architect and AI Enablement Lead at Aflac, argues that the gap between an agent demo and production is control: who the agent is, what it may touch, and what happens when it goes wrong. His answer is four steps in the path of every call (identity, scoped grant, policy gate, audit) and a ten-item checklist to run before anything ships.

"You can swap the model and keep the same risk.", Shanker Valipireddy said at Conf42 MLOps 2026. He speaks as a platform person: more than twenty years in software and data, including a migration of twenty thousand data pipelines that he says saved about three million dollars in licences. His lens is that an agent is a caller on your platform, and should be treated like one.

Why "regulated" changes the design

Four things. The data cannot be leaked, guessed or shown to the wrong caller, so access is the design and not a setting. Some actions need a human to agree before they happen; a log entry saying it already happened is not an approval. Audit must show who did it, when and under which approval, exactly. And a named person is accountable, because an agent has no judgment and no accountability.

A shared service account tells you nothing

Identity comes first because everything else hangs off it. One identity per agent, carrying an owner, a purpose and a scope. When three agents share an account, the audit trail says the account did it, and you cannot stop one without stopping all. Revocation is his test: if killing a misbehaving agent means breaking four others, you will hesitate, and hesitation is how a small problem runs for hours. His rule from the slide: "If you cannot name the caller, you cannot trust the call"

The grant then says what that caller may do this time. Scoped to the data and tools the task needs, timed to expire when the task ends, issued per task. Standing access is how one wrong input becomes a large incident. Narrow the reach and shorten the time, and the same wrong input is a contained error you can explain.

The agent never grades its own homework

The policy gate sits outside the agent and sorts actions into three bands. Low risk and reversible: auto-approve and log. Medium risk: approve, with a tighter scope and a shorter grant. High risk or irreversible: stop and escalate to a human. The risk comes from the action and the data, never from the agent's own view. And the bands get written down before shipping, because bands that live in reviewers' heads get drawn in different places, which you discover during an incident.

Every tool call and data operation is then recorded immutably: which agent, which grant, which policy decision, which human. His audit test is practical. Pick an old run at random and rebuild it from the record alone. If you have to guess at any step, the record is not finished. And there are no side doors: a tool that can be called directly will be, usually under pressure.

Evaluation blocks promotion or it is a report

An agent ships only after passing evaluation, enforced by the platform the way a failed test blocks a release. If a failing result can be noted, discussed and shipped anyway, you have a report people read on the way to shipping. Regression evaluation runs on every change to the model, the prompt, the tools or the data access, and on a schedule, because the agent approved three months ago is not quite the agent running today.

Observability answers three questions in order: what it did, why (the grant, the policy decision, the inputs), and where it stopped. If a run stops at step 14, you need step 14.

Reviewers sleep

What goes wrong mid-run is ordinary systems failure. Data changes under the agent. A tool fails halfway and nobody knows which half is done. A stuck agent loops, and every repeat writes or charges again. His controls are scoped grants, step limits and a kill switch. None of them make the agent smarter. They make its mistakes cheaper.

Then the 2 a.m. question. If the design assumes a reviewer is always there, it will make its own decision at night, and the wrong one. So high-risk work waits, reversible steps continue under a pre-approved grant, and the run records where it paused and why. He says how work should continue safely when the person is away is an area he is researching, and claims no results.

Rollout goes pilot, then shadow (the agent's actions are compared, not executed), then narrow production. Do not skip shadow because the pilot went well: a pilot is watched closely by definition.

Who should watch

Platform, security and MLOps leads in banks, insurers and healthcare who have to say yes or no to an agent project. There is no demo, no vendor and no incident story from his employer; it is a reference pattern delivered slide by slide. If you already run per-agent identity and risk-banded approvals, the evaluation-as-gate and unattended-pause sections are the parts to watch.

entry.title: Your agent's refund check trusts an order ID the model picked
entry.summary: Danila Redikultsev (Aeroclub) at Conf42 MLOps 2026 on self-signed evidence: code checks that pass because the LLM agent chose the value they read.
entry.content:
A customer asked for one specific flight, the agent bought a ticket on a different one, and every check in the code said yes. That is the opening of the talk by Danila Redikultsev, senior software engineer for AI at Aeroclub, at Conf42 MLOps 2026. His diagnosis has a name, self-signed evidence: a field the check trusts, written by the system the check is supposed to be checking. Moving the decision from the prompt into code does not help if the code reads an ID the model chose.

Two blenders, three green checks, one wrong refund

To study it safely he rebuilt the failure in an invented store. A customer writes that their blender arrived broken. The LLM support agent finds two orders for the same blender, 180 dollars each, proposes order 1187 and asks. The customer says yes. Plain code then checks the policy: the order belongs to the customer, it was delivered within 30 days, it is under the 200 dollar limit. All green. The money goes out.

The broken blender was order 1042, delivered 70 days earlier and too old to refund. The second one was its replacement. Nobody attacked anything and the customer did not lie.

Look at where each value came from. The owner came from the database, the delivery date from the carrier, the amount from the order record. The order ID came from the model. The carrier gave the right date for the wrong order.

"A check proves only what the agent could not shape," Danila Redikultsev said at Conf42 MLOps 2026. He borrows two comparisons: a browser rejects a self-signed certificate even when the math is fine, and in banking terms the agent here is both maker and checker.

How often it happens, with honest caveats

He counted published runs of the τ²-bench support-agent benchmark. In the abstract's figures, 82 of 1,632 conversations had the store's tools accept a change to an order the task never asked to change, and in at least 21 the model picked that order itself. Newer models did it less in his own runs: 17 in about 4,000, and in 16 of those the simulated customer had said yes to the agent's summary. He is careful to say that simulated customers show that it happens, not how often.

The most uncomfortable detail is from his rebuilt blender store. The model proposed order 1187 on the grounds that it fell inside the 30-day refund window. It picked the order that would pass the checks.

A second model does not fix it

The obvious patch is an LLM judge. He took 72 wrong refunds and 72 right ones and had Claude Sonnet review them. Reading the agent's own account, the judge approved all 72 wrong ones, even when asked directly whether this was the order the customer meant. Given the whole chat and every order, it caught 50, and it also blocked 41 of the correct refunds. On the cases where the store really lost money, it approved 20 out of 20.

The reason is in the transcript of the chat itself. The customer's yes answers the agent's proposal, so even the conversation is partly written by the system under review. He flags the limits: one judge, his own scenarios, take it as a direction.

Make the check ask who wrote each field

His repair is small. The model may propose an order, but it must point to what the customer wrote. Code checks that the quoted words are in the chat and fit exactly one order. If they fit two, code asks the question itself with options taken straight from the records. In his runs, after a yes to the agent's proposal, 35 refunds out of 180 went to the wrong order. When the choice came from the records, none did. The price was one extra message.

Then he tests the new check, because a new check can be wrong too:

  1. Negative test. Take logged refunds, swap each order ID for another valid order of the same customer, and rerun. The plain policy check stayed green on every swap. Only the check that reads the customer's choice turned red.
  2. Fault injection. Tell the agent not to ask. Wrong refunds went 30 out of 30. With code asking, none.
  3. Shadow mode. Run the new check beside the old one, log what it would block, and have a support lead label a sample against the order records. Only then may it block. If the same model labels the reference set, you are back where you started.

He closes with four questions for any action that costs money or trust: who decides, who writes the words the customer reads, who wrote each field, and who checked the check. He also credits the lineage. In 1988 Norm Hardy called it the confused deputy, a program with authority acting on a name someone else gave it. The homework fits on a sticky note: list every value your final check reads, write next to it whether the database, the customer or the model produced it, swap one, and rerun. "Better to learn that from your logs than from your customer."

Who should watch

Engineers whose agents issue refunds, make bookings or move money, and anyone who has reported guardrail coverage as a percentage. It is about 15 minutes, tightly scripted, and the experiments are his own small-scale runs, which he says plainly. If your agent only reads and summarises, the stakes are lower but the swap test is still worth an afternoon.

entry.title: Put AI compliance in the pipeline, not in a pre-launch meeting
entry.summary: Arpita Sheth at Conf42 MLOps 2026 on AI compliance as code: risk labels at registration, required lineage, policy gates and generated documentation.
entry.content:
An auditor emails you three questions: what data trained the model in production right now, who approved it, and how has it behaved since launch? Arpita Sheth, a staff AI engineer, opens her Conf42 MLOps 2026 talk with that thought experiment and notes that for a lot of teams the answer takes days, sometimes weeks. Her fix is to make compliance behave like tests: the policy is the rule, the pipeline writes the evidence on every run, and a failed check stops a deployment the way a failed test blocks a merge.

The model you reviewed is not the one in production

Her running example is a model that helps screen job applications. Before launch it got a proper review: legal signed off and the bias tests looked fine. Then it retrains weekly on new applications. Someone on another team changes how years of experience is calculated in the feature store. Nobody calls that a release, so nobody calls the review team. Six months later the production model is a different model. "It just has the same name," Arpita Sheth said at Conf42 MLOps 2026.

The review was accurate when it happened and stopped being true the week after. Nobody runs unit tests once before launch and calls it done, and compliance can work the same way. "The policy is the rule, and the pipeline produces the proof."

On why now, she keeps the legal part short. The EU AI Act sorts systems by risk, a hiring model counts as high risk, and what the law asks for reads like an MLOps backlog: know your data, keep technical documentation, log what the system does, keep a human involved, monitor after launch. In the US, many companies follow the voluntary NIST AI Risk Management Framework while state rules keep changing. And under GDPR, a deletion request means knowing which models learned from that person's data.

Five layers, read from the bottom up

None of it needs new infrastructure. You already have a model registry, metadata, CI/CD and monitoring.

Risk classification at registration. The team answers a few questions: what is the model for, does it use personal or sensitive data, does it make the final call on a person. Hiring plus a decision about a person means high risk, which brings more checks, more documentation and a required human sign-off. Keep it as clear rules with a person confirming the result, because a model labelled low risk by mistake quietly switches off every later check.

Lineage. Every training run writes down which data and version it used, which features and how they were calculated, which code, and the results, along with consent and delete-by details. It is written while training happens, not pieced together from old chat threads. With it, the deletion question becomes a query that takes seconds. Her rule: a run that does not record its lineage fails.

Policy gates. One before training: may we use this data for this purpose, did unexpected personal information sneak in, is anything past its delete-by date? One before deployment: does the model meet the fairness bar, is the documentation complete, has a person signed off? Then the lesson she says she learned the hard way: "A gate that just says policy violation is kind of useless." If engineers do not know why it failed or how to fix it, they will find a way around it.

Monitoring. Drift alerts saved as dated records, fairness measured in production, and sampled prediction logs with the model version. Put a delete date on the logs or the audit trail becomes its own privacy problem.

Documentation. With the first four layers working, the pipeline fills in a template for every model version. People write only the judgment parts: what the model is for and how humans can step in.

LLM features use the same layers with more in them

Add an LLM that summarises each resume and lineage grows: the base model and its version, any fine-tuning data, the prompt version and the documents retrieved. A small prompt edit can change behaviour as much as a retrain, so prompts get versioned like code. The gate becomes a test suite run before every release: harmful content, leaked personal information, instruction override, made-up facts.

Thresholds are a negotiation

Her lessons from building such systems at scale are the part worth replaying. Start at registration, not with the dashboard. Record data history from day one, since adding it later is like trying to find the receipt for something you bought a year ago. And agree thresholds jointly. Set by compliance alone they are too strict and engineers quietly build side pipelines. Set by engineering alone they are too loose and you are exposed in an audit.

She admits the costs: gates slow teams down, and one fairness bar will not fit every model. Her answers include the same dashboard for compliance and engineering, and an exception path that is a logged temporary override with an expiry date, so the exception itself becomes evidence.

Her test for next week: pick your highest-risk model and ask which data trained the version in production. If you can answer with a query, you are in good shape. "If it takes a meeting, that's where to start."

Who should watch

ML platform leads, governance engineers and anyone whose model retrains more often than legal meets. It is a concept talk with one worked example and no tooling demo. Teams with lineage and gates already in place can skip to the trade-offs near the end.

entry.title: Grade the agent on what the service recorded, not on its reply
entry.summary: Sajal Garg (Microsoft AI) at Conf42 MLOps 2026 on agent evals that compare the reply, the tool actions and the service state before a release decision.
entry.content:
An agent's reply tells you what it claims. Its tool calls tell you what it tried. Only the service tells you what changed. At Conf42 MLOps 2026, Sajal Garg, Principal Software Engineer at Microsoft AI, follows one small request from a normal run through planted failures to a release decision, and shows why an update with nicer writing scores still gets blocked. Every job, trace and score in the talk is a hand-constructed teaching example, which he says up front.

One task, four boxes, three records

The task: prepare a training job, wait for approval, submit it once, then return its real job ID and current status. Four actors stay on screen the whole time: the user, the assistant, a job tool that can create or look up jobs, and the training service. Approval is stored separately, because an assistant saying the user approved cannot create permission.

Sajal pins down success before running anything. It needs one matching accepted job, its real ID, and a reply that matches the observed status. Submitted does not mean finished. Reporting "submitted and queued" satisfies the task; reporting that training finished needs evidence of completion. And seeing job A in the reply does not rule out an unseen second job, so the check reads the service's record.

To make this repeatable he adds a test runner and a checker. Each attempt starts in a fresh sandbox, the expectation is fixed before the run, and both the current build and the updated build get the same four cases: approved work, no approval, a lost reply, and a result too uncertain for another write. "The reply is an input to check, not its own answer key," Sajal Garg said at Conf42 MLOps 2026.

A harmless message can sit on top of an unauthorized job

In the no-approval case he plants a defect in the tool that skips the approval check. The tool sends the create request, the service accepts a job, and the assistant returns a calm message that the plan is ready. The check expected zero accepted jobs and found one. The friendly reply cannot cancel the effect, and the build is blocked.

He also separates facts from prose. A writing rubric gives points for a findable ID and status, plain language and a clear next action, but a failed or unknown factual check gets no style score at all. If the writing judge has an outage, the reply is unscored and the execution evidence stands.

A timeout is missing knowledge

The lost-reply case is the one most teams will recognise. The first create request is accepted as job A, the test drops the service's reply, and the assistant sees a timeout. After a restart, the updated build creates again and the service accepts job B. The assistant then reports that it submitted one job. The independent observer sees two accepted IDs.

The corrected recovery looks up the original operation before any new write. If the lookup is unreliable, an empty search does not prove rejection. A retry needs valid approval plus either a real provider guarantee against duplicates or authoritative proof that the first request was not accepted. When time runs out without a safe answer, the right behaviour is to pause further writes and say what remains unknown.

Clean evidence takes more than clearing the chat. Each trial needs isolated service state, approval records and deduplication history, and a trial is not closed just because the assistant returned: a pending request could still create a job after you declared a pass.

Block, hold or pass, and missing scores are never zeros

In the comparison ledger, four cases run twice each, so eight attempts per build. The current build satisfies all eight. The updated build satisfies four, with an unauthorized job, a duplicate and two unknown outcomes among the rest, while its writing average looks better on a smaller rated subset. A known unauthorized or duplicate job means block. Missing required evidence without a known critical failure means hold. Neither is a pass, and a better writing average cannot buy back a duplicate job.

After the fix, the retest satisfies all eight, which supports a limited pilot and nothing broader. The imagined pilot then finds a case the suite missed: the job count is right, the service says queued, and the assistant tells the user training finished. "Queuing is not a failure, misreporting it is," as Sajal puts it. The new test pairs a queued example with a succeeded one, so a lazy fix that always answers "queued" fails too. The suite grows to twelve attempts and the loop repeats.

Who should watch

Engineers who own evals or release gates for tool-using agents, especially where an action costs money or cannot be undone. entry.title: Prompt Engineering Conference London treats prompts as production code
entry.summary: Prompt Engineering Conference London, November 26 - Wise, AWS, IBM, Red Buffer and Superagentic AI on releasing, testing and judging prompts. CONF42 = 42% off.

The Prompt Engineering Conference comes to London on November 26, 2026, with three tracks and roughly thirty talks that treat a prompt the way you would treat a config change: versioned, rolled out, tested and occasionally rolled back. A prompt rollout can be an incident

The talk to circle first is Ritesh Modi (Wise), Prompt Release Engineering. His abstract describes a 5% rollout of a prompt and model configuration that silently stayed in production for five months. If you have ever left a feature flag at 5% and forgotten it, you already know how that story feels, and the talk is about the release discipline that stops it.

Emmanuela Opurum (SoftNet Technologies) comes at the same problem from the architecture side with Designing Production-Grade Prompt Systems for AI Agents: A Solution Architect's Perspective: why prompt setups that work in a notebook fall over once they meet production.

Who writes the next prompt?

Guilherme Santos (Blindsight) follows the other thread in Prompt Lawyering. How AI games human requests, starting from the Tetris-playing AI that learned to pause the game so it could never lose. Specification gaming, now with your system prompt.

Egor Grositskiy (Beat Saber) brings an art director's view in When Prompting Isn't Enough, where the hard part is defining "better" for creative output at all.

Judging output you cannot check

  • Olushola Oladipupo (AWS), Before Your Agent Takes Action: Evaluating Customer-Service AI, for agents that can change records, not just answer.

  • Peter Fox (IBM) on regression-testing a virtual assistant's migration from rules to LLM orchestration.

entry.title: An AUC of 0.96 that missed more than half the real cases
entry.summary: Deborah Adedigba (UK Ministry of Defence) at Conf42 MLOps 2026 on what her skin lesion classifier taught her about metrics, validation and negative results.
entry.content:
Two of Deborah Adedigba's skin lesion models scored a precision around 0.95 and an AUC of 0.96 on smartphone photos, with a recall of 0.44. They were usually right when they flagged something, and they missed more than half of the real cases. At Conf42 MLOps 2026, the Data Scientist at the UK Ministry of Defence uses her own MSc dissertation and the journal paper that followed as a case study in the question she wishes she had asked earlier: when a model scores well, what do you need to see before anyone relies on it?

The stakes explain the choice of metric. Citing Globocan, she puts melanoma at around 325,000 new cases and 57,000 deaths a year. Caught early, five-year survival is around 99 percent. Caught after it has spread, around 27 percent. A screening model that misses cases is failing at the one job it has.

No model won on both datasets

The project compared a custom CNN against transfer learning with ResNet50, VGG16, EfficientNet and Inception-ResNet-V2, built in TensorFlow and Keras on Google Colab and Kaggle GPUs. She used two datasets on purpose: dermoscopic images from ISIC, magnified and fairly standardised, and smartphone photographs with six lesion classes, where image quality and size vary. Melanoma, the target, had just 52 images in the second set.

On dermoscopic images EfficientNet led with about 0.85 accuracy and an AUC of 0.9, ResNet and VGG16 sat around 0.75, and the custom CNN's AUC was 0.52, which she calls a coin flip. On smartphone photos the order changed: ResNet50 was best at around 0.75 accuracy and EfficientNet dropped to 0.61. Had she tested on one dataset, she says, she would have drawn the wrong conclusion about which model to use.

And then the recall. The headline numbers looked fine while the screening failure sat underneath. Her conclusion is that reliable ML needs a set of metrics chosen for the risk, and a single number can hide exactly the failure you care about.

Two things broke, and both were worth reporting

The first was unstable training. Loss jumped around and accuracy was poor, so she tried undersampling the large classes to fix the imbalance. It backfired: accuracy fell from around 54.7 percent to somewhere between 24 and 40 percent. What turned it around was augmentation, standardised preprocessing, a lower learning rate and SMOTE to synthesise examples of rare classes. She only knew which change did what because she was tracking metrics per experiment.

The second was U-Net. The idea was to segment the lesion so the classifier would ignore hair, rulers and surrounding skin. It did not help, possibly because segmentation removed context the model was using, and she took it out. Her lesson: "every stage should prove its value", and a negative result belongs in the write-up.

The dissertation's numbers were a hypothesis

She is direct about how far the first results can be trusted. One train and test split, no cross-validation, no external test set, and SMOTE applied before the split, so there was a chance of leakage. None of that makes the work worthless, she says. It makes the result a hypothesis.

The follow-up paper fixed the process. Stratified five-fold cross-validation with repeated seeds. A class-weighted loss so mistakes on rare cases cost more. Accuracy replaced by macro F1 and the Matthews correlation coefficient, which stay honest on skewed data. Augmentation applied to training data only. McNemar's test to check whether two models make different errors, plus an ablation study. Saved weights and out-of-fold predictions instead of results copied by hand. Explanations moved from saliency maps fed into the model to Grad-CAM and Grad-CAM++ heat maps, adapted for CNNs and transformers, to catch a model staring at a ruler.

The ensemble in that paper reached a macro F1 of 0.998. She still does not oversell it, because the external test set is still missing and the heat maps were not validated against a dermatologist. "internally consistent, not independently validated", Deborah Adedigba said at Conf42 MLOps 2026, adding that the paper says so too.

Five questions before a model goes near users

Her takeaway list is short. Can I rebuild this result from versioned data and code? Is evaluation independent of training data? Do I know where it fails and for whom? Will I know when it degrades? Can a clinician, or whichever expert applies, see why it predicted what it did?

Who should watch

Data scientists and ML engineers moving from notebooks to anything with consequences, and students about to write up a dissertation with one impressive number in it. It is an honest research retrospective. The model never left a Streamlit demo, so do not expect serving, monitoring or CI detail, and the talk's datasets and figures differ somewhat from the abstract. The before-and-after of the evaluation method is the reason to watch.

  • MLOps at Scale: Designing Governed AI Pipelines for Healthcare Impact by Nikitha Edulakanti of Fresenius Medical Care at Conf42 MLOps 2025.

entry.title: Filtering throws away 96.94% of the web, and that's the point
entry.summary: Nicolo Brandizzi (Fraunhofer IAIS) at Conf42 MLOps 2026 on turning 173 billion Common Crawl documents into LLM training data, with the CPU and euro bills.
entry.content:
Run deduplication before filtering and the job costs 750 CPU years instead of 25. That single reordering is the most memorable number in the talk Nicolo Brandizzi, senior research scientist at Fraunhofer IAIS, gave at Conf42 MLOps 2026. He co-leads the data team there, and he walks through how the OpenGPT-X project, which produced the open Teuken models, turned 173 billion web documents into a training corpus. It is pitched as a beginner's tour and it is one, with real bills attached.

Two sources, one record format

Training data comes in two kinds. Curated sources such as books, encyclopedias and parliament transcripts have been through an editorial process. Web data, meaning Common Crawl, is enormous and mostly low value: an article body surrounded by ads, footers and navigation.

The curated pipeline is light: format conversion, content normalization, language detection, metadata normalization, some filtering. His example of why normalization matters is the word café. The accented e can be one character or a plain e plus a combining accent. They look identical to you and the tokenizer sees two different words.

The web pipeline starts from Common Crawl's WET files, chosen over WARC because some HTML noise is already removed, and adds quality scoring, harmful content detection, a cheap pre-filter, heavier filtering and finally deduplication. Both paths end in the same JSONL record: the text plus metadata about source, language and scores. His first takeaway is to keep that lineage, so that when an evaluation result moves you can trace it back to the config change that caused it.

1.2 million years of reading

The raw input was 173 billion documents, about 700 terabytes from 60 Common Crawl dumps. The abstract gives the share removed as 96.94%. About five billion documents remain.

To show that this is the pipeline working, he converts it to reading time. A person reading at average speed would need around 1.2 million years for the full set, which he notes is four times longer than our species has existed. The five billion survivors still take 35,000 years, roughly the age of the oldest cave paintings. Plenty left.

The cheap filters that do much of the removal do not understand text at all. Count words per line and keep lines above four. Count symbols and keep documents under 30%. That is enough to keep an article and drop a navigation menu and a log dump.

Order is a cost decision

Add up every step and the pipeline took 31 years of single-core CPU time. Deduplication, done locally with MinHash and LSH, accounts for 80% of it, about 25 of the 31 years. That is why it sits last, after filtering has shrunk the input. Swap the order and deduplication alone needs 750 CPU years, more than thirty times as much.

"the order is a cost decision and it matters," Nicolo Brandizzi said at Conf42 MLOps 2026.

Then he complicates it. CPU time and wall-clock time are different budgets. Measured in terabytes processed per day, the slowest steps were downloading and filtering, and since the steps run in series the slowest one sets the calendar. Add euros and you have three variables, compute, money and calendar days, that influence each other and that a project has to plan for from the start.

Form is cheap to check, value is not

The cheap filters have a blind spot. A paragraph on photosynthesis and a line of cheap-flight spam both pass, because both are well formed. Meanwhile code or translator-style notes with many symbols can be dropped despite being valuable. Filters see form. Value needs a reader.

The current answer is an LLM as judge, rating each document from zero to five. He prices it: about 300 euros per million documents at mid-2026 rates, which comes to around 1.5 million euros for the five billion. Too much.

So the last part is about proxies. His framing: "bad text and bad quality data is easy to spot and good is not". Good depends on what the model is for. He describes a trust ladder with human reviewers on top (most trusted, most expensive), LLM judges in the middle and heuristics at the bottom (nearly free, blind to value). The work is passing trust downward: humans calibrate the judge, the judge labels a sample, and cheaper filters are learned from those labels. He cites FineWeb's educational-value score as one such proxy. There is no magic formula, he says, and any quality score is only confirmed after training, at evaluation.

Who should watch

Engineers and researchers who use pretrained models or Hugging Face datasets and have never seen how the text got there. People who already run web-scale data pipelines will find it introductory, though the CPU-year and euro figures are worth having as reference points. The delivery is unhurried and the slides carry references for the deduplication comparison.

Related Conf42 talks

  • Beyond Pre-training: Scaling Cloud-Native LLMs with Contextual Data for Real-Time AI by Ankit Awasthi, what happens to data after pre-training.
  • Fine-tuning LLMs: A Cost-Benefit Analysis for Businesses by Muddassar Sharif, another talk that puts money next to model work.
  • Building Efficient and Frugal Image Data Processing Pipelines by Anna Heng Chi, frugal data pipelines in a different modality.
